title: Polymer clay cloisonne-style enamel brooch
subtitle: A black-outlined colour-fill brooch that mimics enamel jewellery
excerpt: A cloisonne-style brooch is a flat polymer clay piece with raised black outlines that form enclosed colour cells, filled with tinted clay to mimic the look of fired enamel. No kiln is needed: the finished brooch sets in a domestic oven. Intermediate makers can build a complex layered piece in one sitting.
sourceNotes: Cloisonne enamel technique references drawn from V&A open-access collection historical metalwork records. Polymer clay adaptation derived from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: A decorative technique in which metal or clay outlines divide a surface into enclosed cells, each filled with coloured enamel or tinted clay
Kneading polymer clay by hand until warm and pliable, removing air pockets and making the clay smooth enough to roll thin
The base layer of clay that supports all surface decoration and carries the brooch pin finding

content.text: A
cloisonne

-style brooch is a flat wearable piece about 4-5 cm across, built in polymer clay with raised black outlines and filled colour cells that mimic enamel jewellery. Polymer clay sets in a domestic oven, so no kiln is needed. An intermediate maker with tinted clay in four or five colours can build a brooch with a repeating geometric or floral design in one session.

materials.name: Strong adhesive suitable for cured polymer clay
Liquid polymer clay or varnish for sealing

content.text: Preparation

Plan your design on paper first. Sketch a 4-5 cm shape: oval, teardrop, shield, or free-form. Divide it into 6-12 enclosed cells using lines that all connect to each other or to the outer edge. Cells with no exit are hard to fill neatly. Choose colours that contrast with the black outlines: jewel tones, pastels, or earthy neutrals all work.
Conditioning
each colour block before rolling saves time during construction.
Building the brooch

Roll a sheet of black polymer clay 2 mm thick using the pottery rolling pin with guide strips on each side to keep thickness even. Cut the outer brooch shape from this sheet with the fettling knife. This is the back plate.
Lay the
back plate
flat on a tile or piece of baking parchment. This will go directly into the oven later, so keep it on a baking-safe surface throughout.

Roll black clay into thin ropes, 1-1.5 mm in diameter. To make an even rope, roll a short sausage between your palms first, then roll it out on a smooth surface under your fingers, working outward from the centre. Cut lengths as you need them.

Following your sketch, lay the black ropes onto the back plate to form the outline cells. Press each rope gently into the surface so it bonds without squashing flat. Where two ropes meet, press the join firmly and smooth with a dampened fingertip. All cell boundaries must touch the outer edge or another boundary to close the cell.

Run the needle tool along the inside base of each cell wall to press the rope down fully. The walls should sit proud of the back plate by 1-1.5 mm when finished. Use a wooden rib to gently press the tops of the walls flat without distorting their position.

Roll each fill colour into a thin sheet, about 1 mm thick. Cut pieces slightly larger than each cell. Lay a piece of fill clay over its cell and press gently into the interior, filling the cell to the level of the top of the walls. The fill clay should sit flush with or very slightly above the top of the black walls.

Trim any overflow from one cell before filling the adjacent cell. Use the fettling knife to cut flush against the wall on the filled side. Work from the centre of the design outward to avoid distorting completed cells.

Once all cells are filled, lay a piece of smooth parchment over the front of the brooch. Press very gently with a flat wooden rib across the whole surface to level the fill and push out any air trapped under the colour pieces. Remove the parchment carefully.
Check the outer edge of the brooch is clean and the back plate is visible at the edge. Trim any colour fill that has crept over the edge with the fettling knife. Smooth the cut edge with a fingertip.

Cure in a domestic oven according to the clay manufacturer's temperature and time guidelines, typically 110-130 degrees C for 15-30 minutes depending on thickness. Use a digital oven thermometer: home oven dials are often 10-20 degrees out. Place the brooch on a tile or folded index card to keep the surface flat and avoid scorching.

After curing and cooling fully, sand the front surface through the grits (400, then 800) if you want a smooth, polished enamel look. Wipe clean. Apply a thin coat of liquid polymer clay or compatible varnish to seal the surface and add sheen. Cure or dry per the product instructions.

Attach the brooch pin finding to the back of the cured piece using a strong adhesive. Allow to cure fully before wearing. Position the pin in the upper third of the back so the brooch hangs level on fabric.
Care

Polymer clay is durable when fully cured but can flex and crack under sharp impact. Do not place in a microwave or dishwasher. Wipe clean with a dry cloth. Store flat or pinned to a padded surface to protect the cell walls from being bent.
Variations

For a stained-glass window effect, use translucent polymer clay tinted with small amounts of coloured clay for the fill. The translucent base lets light through at the edges of each cell, making the colour glow when held to a window.
Scale the design up to a 7-8 cm pendant shape with a loop of black clay pressed into the top before curing. Larger cells are more forgiving for beginners and the design reads well at pendant scale.

Try a two-tone fill: lay two thin ropes of different colours side by side in a wide cell, then press flat together. The join blurs at the edges, producing a gradient within each cell without blending the clays.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Cell walls collapse inward when fill is pressed in
items.cause: The ropes were too thin (under 1 mm) or were not pressed fully onto the back plate before filling
items.fix: Remove the fill clay and re-press the rope walls before refilling. Use 1.5 mm ropes for designs with wide cells

items.problem: Colour fill pulls away from the wall on curing
items.cause: The fill clay was not pressed firmly enough into the corners of the cell, leaving a small air gap that opens during heating
items.fix: After filling each cell, run a needle tool around the inner base of the wall to press the fill into the junction. Re-flatten the surface with parchment

items.problem: Black outlines look grey after curing
items.cause: The black clay was under-cured or mixed with another colour during conditioning
items.fix: Increase oven temperature by 5 degrees and cure for 5 more minutes. Use a dedicated conditioning mat and clean hands when handling black clay

items.problem: Surface is uneven with ridges across the cells
items.cause: Fill clay pieces were not pressed level with the top of the walls before curing
items.fix: Sand the cured surface with 400-grit sandpaper using circular motions under water. Progress to 800-grit for a smooth finish, then varnish

items.problem: Brooch pin falls off after wearing
items.cause: The adhesive was not fully cured before the brooch was used, or an incompatible adhesive was chosen
items.fix: Use two-part epoxy or a cyanoacrylate gel rated for plastic. Allow the full adhesive cure time (often 24 hours) before wearing
